lesson.title: The Hunger Alarm: Ghrelin and the Drive to Eat
lesson.summary: Ghrelin is a hormone released mainly by the stomach when it is empty, signaling the hypothalamus to stimulate appetite and prepare the body to eat. Often called the hunger hormone, it works opposite leptin's fullness signal, and together the two help regulate when and how much a person eats.
lesson.body:
If leptin is the body's long range fullness signal, ghrelin is its short range hunger alarm. Ghrelin is produced primarily by cells lining the stomach, and its levels rise noticeably when the stomach is empty, typically climbing in the hours before a person's usual mealtime and then falling sharply once food has been eaten. This rhythm tends to track fairly closely with a person's habitual eating schedule, rising and falling in a pattern the body comes to anticipate rather than waiting passively for a meal to happen to arrive.

This anticipatory quality is part of what makes ghrelin distinct among the hormones covered in this sequence. The stress hormone cortisol, described earlier as part of the HPA axis, mainly responds to events after they happen, but ghrelin's rhythm is shaped in large part by learned mealtime habits themselves, which is one reason hunger can appear right on schedule even on a day when a planned meal ends up delayed.

Like leptin, ghrelin travels through the bloodstream to reach the hypothalamus, the same general target region described throughout this run of hormone chapters, where it binds receptors on neurons that stimulate appetite. This is essentially the mirror image of what leptin does: where leptin activates circuits that suppress hunger, ghrelin activates circuits that promote it, and the two hormones function together something like opposite ends of a seesaw balancing the drive to eat against the signal to stop.

That contrast is worth stating plainly. Leptin, released by fat tissue, reports on long term energy sufficiency and suppresses appetite when reserves are adequate. Ghrelin, released by an empty stomach, reports on immediate, short term need and stimulates appetite until a meal arrives. Healthy regulation of eating behavior depends on both of these signals reaching the hypothalamus reliably and in the right balance, rather than on either hormone acting alone.

Sleep offers a useful everyday illustration of how these two systems interact. When sleep is chronically restricted, the body's hormonal balance tends to shift in a way that favors increased hunger: ghrelin levels tend to rise while leptin levels tend to fall, producing a combined signal that promotes greater appetite and calorie intake than the person would otherwise experience. This shift is one of several proposed explanations for why persistent poor sleep is often associated with weight gain over time, alongside other behavioral factors like having more waking hours available for eating.

Ghrelin has some secondary roles under continued study as well, including possible involvement in reward related eating behavior and, consistent with its name, in triggering the release of growth hormone from the pituitary gland. Its clearest and most firmly established behavioral role, though, remains its most straightforward one: it is the signal that gets an empty stomach's message to the brain and starts the search for food.
